entries.clue: Primarily, the affluent Jahan's mausoleum; Agra's heart; architecturally luxe? (3,5)

definitions.text: Primarily, the affluent Jahan's mausoleum; Agra's heart; architecturally luxe?

indicators.note: what comes first in each word is what counts

blocks.clueFragment: the affluent Jahan's mausoleum; Agra's heart; architecturally luxe
blocks.note: first letter of each of the eight words

annotation.surface: A guidebook's breathless description of India's most famous tomb.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition. 'Heart' here is just part of the description, not an instruction to take middle letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes the white marble tomb the emperor Shah Jahan built for his wife at Agra, the jewel of the city.

entries.clue: Loudly convey approval of that proof of payment (6)

indicators.note: said out loud, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: to tick something is to mark it as approved

annotation.surface: An inspector nodding through someone's receipt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That' stands for 'it', so approving that is 'tick it'.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the slip you are handed for a train or a show is your evidence that you paid.

entries.clue: Spy having problems concealing bit of electrical connector (5,4)

indicators.note: to conceal something is to hold it hidden inside, so the first word wraps the letter
only a small part, the first letter, of 'electrical' is used

annotation.surface: A spy in trouble while tampering with a piece of wiring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Electrical connector' reads as one piece of hardware, but the two words are split between two jobs.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Ian Fleming's 007 is the best-known fictional spy.

entries.clue: Australian yearns for starters of halloumi and harissa (7)

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for Australian

annotation.surface: An Australian craving Middle Eastern appetisers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starters' looks like a menu word but it means the first letters: halloumi and harissa both start with H.
annotation.definitionFit: Both foods begin with the letter H, and the name of that letter spelt out is aitch, so two of them make the plural.

entries.clue: Not one for one, but 1 for one (6,7)

definitions.text: Not one for one, but 1 for one

blocks.note: the surface reads 'one' as a person; the setter means the letter-like Roman symbol I, which stands for one and is ruled out
the digit itself is the sign used for the number one in everyday counting

annotation.walkthrough: The Roman numeral I is excluded; the figure 1 is the kind of numeral that came to Europe via Arabic mathematics.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by contrast: the digit 1, as opposed to Roman I, is the everyday symbol system we write numbers in.

entries.clue: Central parts in clue needing editing (6)

indicators.note: the letters are to be changed about

annotation.surface: A setter noticing the middle of a crossword clue needs a rewrite.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link joining definition to wordplay, but it is two of the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the core of a cell, an atom or a group is its centre, and the plural gives central parts.

entries.clue: A little bug lies twitching, extremely unpleasant (7)

indicators.note: only a small part of the following words is used

annotation.surface: A small insect lying on its back, legs twitching, horrible to see.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A little bug' reads as a small insect, but 'a little' is the instruction to take part of the words that follow.
annotation.definitionFit: The superlative of ugly, which can mean unpleasant (an ugly mood), so 'extremely' supplies the -est.

entries.clue: Many around university displaying yoga position (5)

indicators.note: placed all round, so the word for many surrounds the university letter

annotation.surface: A crowd of students around a campus showing off their yoga.
annotation.walkthrough: U for university is a standard abbreviation, as on British maps and in degree lists.
annotation.definitionFit: Named example: the cross-legged seated pose, feet on thighs, is named after the water flower.

entries.clue: The writer's threat to describe a sovereign (8)

indicators.note: to describe is to draw around, so the threat is drawn around A

blocks.note: the writer is 'I', and 'the writer's' = I am = I'M
goes inside PERIL, before its last letter: PERI(A)L

annotation.surface: An author threatening to write a portrait of a monarch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Describe' in the geometric sense means to draw a line round something, which is why it can signal a container.
annotation.definitionFit: Adjective sense: sovereign power is supreme and royal, the rank of an emperor.

entries.clue: Park up as we do here. (4,2,1,4,4) (4,2,1,4,4)

blocks.note: a driver parking up brings the car to a halt
the clue itself ends at a printed period

annotation.surface: A driving instructor telling a learner to pull in here.
annotation.walkthrough: The dot after 'here' is part of the clue: the sentence literally ends there, and full stop is British for a period.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom covering both senses: a car halting completely, and a sentence ending at its punctuation mark.

entries.clue: Pitifully yelped, mourned being made little use of (13)

indicators.note: badly done, so the letters are in a sorry state

annotation.surface: Someone crying out and grieving over being overlooked.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's grief makes 'Pitifully' look like it describes the yelping; it only describes what happens to the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a worker given too few hours or too little to do is being made little use of.

entries.clue: Uncomprehending utterances: Cockney confusion (3)

blocks.note: the grunts you make when you haven't followed
the stock puzzled exclamation of a Cockney speaker

annotation.surface: Blank looks and grunts from a Londoner who has lost the thread.
annotation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner from the East End, whose puzzled 'Eh?' is a caricature staple.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses name the same noise, the questioning grunt of someone who didn't catch or understand.

entries.clue: Locksmith? (11)

blocks.note: the surface reads a tradesman who fits door locks; locks can also be strands of hair
flags that 'smith', a worker, is being applied to the other kind of lock

annotation.walkthrough: A locksmith fixes door locks; the question mark says to read 'locks' as hair.
annotation.definitionFit: Pun: someone who works on locks of hair is a smith of locks.

entries.clue: Spooner's confused about one baddie in whodunnit (8)

indicators.note: mixed up, so the name's letters are jumbled
the jumbled letters go around I

blocks.note: I = one, placed inside the jumble

annotation.surface: The Reverend Spooner muddled over who did it in a murder mystery.
annotation.walkthrough: Spooner usually means a spoonerism is coming; here his name is just seven letters to mix up.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: arsenic in the tea is a classic villain's method in detective fiction.

entries.clue: Opera coat's fashionable (5)

indicators.note: fashioned, made into a new shape

annotation.surface: An evening coat that's the height of style for a night at the opera.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opera coat' looks like one garment; 'Opera' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Puccini's 1900 work is one of the best-known operas.

entries.clue: Boss on gymnastic equipment that's valuable in stable (4,5)

blocks.note: a boss is a stud, a round knob on a surface
the vaulting horse or pommel horse

annotation.surface: A gymnast's apparatus prized by a stable of athletes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boss' wants to be a manager; it is the raised knob on a shield. 'On' places the first piece above the second in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Cryptic-ish description: a stallion kept for breeding earns fees, so it is the prize asset of a stable.

entries.clue: Repugnance as staidest put out (8)

indicators.note: disturbed, so the letters are displaced

annotation.surface: The most prim and proper people annoyed and disgusted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as the staid being annoyed; it is the signal to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, a little milder: both mean a strong feeling of dislike.

entries.clue: I will often become this when spelling things out (5)

definitions.text: I will often become this when spelling things out

blocks.note: the surface reads 'I' as the speaker; the setter means the ninth letter of the alphabet
radio operators and call centres spell words with a code word for each letter

annotation.walkthrough: In the NATO phonetic alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie…) the letter I is said as the name of a country.
annotation.definitionFit: Crossword-only sense: the code word used for the letter I when spelling aloud by radio or phone.

entries.clue: Financial official in German car on rocky outcrop (7)

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor

annotation.surface: An accountant driving an Audi up onto a crag.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the car above the outcrop in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain description: the person who inspects a company's accounts is a financial official.

entries.clue: Flash corporation men will be cutting impetus (8)

indicators.note: the men cut into the other two pieces, splitting them

blocks.note: a mo = a moment, a flash
corporation is old slang for a pot belly, a tum

annotation.surface: Staff pushing into a glitzy company to give it drive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a firm; it is joke slang for a big stomach. 'Flash' is a noun, an instant, not flashy.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both mean the driving force that keeps something moving.

entries.clue: English maniac to write about God (7)

indicators.note: turned about, so the whole string reads backwards

blocks.note: a nut = a maniac, a fanatic

annotation.surface: An English madman scribbling about the deity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'on the subject of' God; it turns the whole assembled string round.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Roman ruler of the sea is one of the gods.

entries.clue: Tyrant to remove blemishes? (6)

blocks.note: a made-up verb: the prefix for undoing, plus the word for a pimple

annotation.surface: A dictator fussing over his complexion.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented verb 'de-spot', to take the spots off.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym for the ruler, and a punning coinage for the skincare sense.

entries.clue: Tremendous roar coming from Earth under Clapham (11)

indicators.note: the answer comes out of the words that follow

annotation.surface: A rumble rising from below Clapham, perhaps a Tube train.
annotation.walkthrough: Clapham is a district of south London with Underground stations beneath it, which is what the surface pictures.
annotation.definitionFit: Description: the single loud crash heard in a storm is a tremendous roar.

entries.clue: Underwater vessel but prow taken from sub (over a ton) (1-4)

indicators.note: the front of the word, like a ship's bow, is removed

annotation.surface: A submarine with its bow shot off, weighing more than a ton.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over a ton' reads as a weight; it is three abbreviations in a row.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the German navy's submarine of both world wars is a vessel that travels underwater.

entries.clue: Tool getting end of gerbil out of cavity (3)

indicators.note: the letter is taken out of the word for cavity

blocks.note: hole = cavity; its L is the one removed

annotation.surface: A gardener's tool used to dig a gerbil out of its burrow.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a pet being extracted from a hole; in fact the pet's last letter is extracted from the hole.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the long-handled blade for weeding is a garden tool.

entries.clue: Troopship loudly goes off to embark on spree of a sort (4,4,3,4)

indicators.note: explodes, so the letters are scattered

annotation.surface: A noisy troop carrier setting sail for a riotous time ashore.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loudly' looks like a sound signal; here it is just six letters of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: the catchphrase names a shopping spree carried on until exhaustion.

entries.clue: Glimpse of Everyman at ultimately inexpensive or unhealthy greasy spoon? (6)

indicators.note: only the first bit of 'Everyman' is seen
the last letter of each of the following words

annotation.surface: The setter spotted at a cheap, unwholesome café.
annotation.walkthrough: A greasy spoon is British slang for a cheap café serving fried food; the question mark marks it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a cheap fry-up café is one kind of place to eat.

entries.clue: A partisan, that woman's overcome by a depression (8)

indicators.note: covered over, so the woman's word sits inside the depression

blocks.note: a dent is a depression in a surface
her = that woman's; goes inside the dent

annotation.surface: A resistance fighter, a woman, overwhelmed by low spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as low mood; it is a physical hollow. 'A partisan' could look like the start of the wordplay, but the A belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a partisan is a committed supporter of a cause or party.
